items.title: PowerRules
items.text:
PowerRules is a rule-based command automation tool: when the conditions of a rule match, its commands run.

Originally built to shut down a computer at the right moment, it now runs any shell command.

WindowsLinux & macOS 
rules:
  # Match when no backup process is running between 23:00 and 01:30
  - name: "Shutdown when no backup is running at night"
    conditions:
      and:
        - process:
            name: "backup.exe"
            exists: false
        - datetime:
            between:
              start: "23"
              end: "1:30"
    actions:
      - run: "shutdown /s /t 0"

rules:
  # Match when no backup process is running between 23:00 and 01:30
  - name: "Shutdown when no backup is running at night"
    conditions:
      and:
        - process:
            name: "backup"
            exists: false
        - datetime:
            between:
              start: "23"
              end: "1:30"
    actions:
      - run: "shutdown -h now"

items.title: How it works
items.text:
• A policy is a YAML file with a list of rules.
  • Each rule has conditions (processes, datetime, etc.) and actions (commands to run).
  • Rules are evaluated from top to bottom. The first rule that matches runs its actions in order.
  • A policy has to be trusted first, so modifications of a policy or its scripts do not go unnoticed.
Why choose PowerRules over scheduled tasks or systemd timers?

You can build the same thing yourself: a scheduled task which runs every few seconds and starts a script containing all the logic. PowerRules is essentially that script partially written. You describe what should happen instead of how to check it.

  • Declarative: Combine conditions with and, or and not in a readable YAML file.
  • Portable: The same policy usually works on Windows, Linux and macOS.
  • Debugging: --dry-run shows what would happen and debug logs explain why a condition did or did not match.

For a single fixed schedule on one system, the built-in tools are usually the simpler choice.

items.title: Actions
items.text:
Summary

Actions are commands which run one after another when a rule matches. If an action fails, the remaining actions are skipped unless continue_on_error is set.

items.title: Example
items.text:
WindowsLinux & macOS 
rules:
  # Match every night from 23:00 until 1:30
  - name: "Backup time"
    conditions:
      datetime:
        between:
          start: "23"
          end: "1:30"
    actions:
      # A failing backup does not prevent the remaining actions
      - name: "Backup"
        run: '.\my-action.ps1'
        working_directory: scripts # Relative to the policy file
        env:
          TARGET: 'D:\backup'
        timeout: 600
        success_exit_codes: [0, 3]
        continue_on_error: true
        trusted_files:
          - scripts/my-action.ps1 # Relative to the policy file (not to working_directory)

      # Fail if the output does not contain "Notification service is ready"
      - name: "Check"
        run: '.\my-check.ps1'
        working_directory: scripts
        stdout:
          value: "Notification service is ready"
          match:
            type: contains
        trusted_files:
          - scripts/my-check.ps1

      # Start a command in the background without waiting for it
      - run: '.\my-notification.ps1'
        working_directory: scripts
        wait: false
        trusted_files:
          - scripts/my-notification.ps1

rules:
  # Match every night from 23:00 until 1:30
  - name: "Backup time"
    conditions:
      datetime:
        between:
          start: "23"
          end: "1:30"
    actions:
      # A failing backup does not prevent the remaining actions
      - name: "Backup"
        run: "./my-action.sh"
        working_directory: scripts # Relative to the policy file
        env:
          TARGET: "/mnt/backup"
        timeout: 600
        success_exit_codes: [0, 3]
        continue_on_error: true
        trusted_files:
          - scripts/my-action.sh # Relative to the policy file (not to working_directory)

      # Fail if the output does not contain "Notification service is ready"
      - name: "Check"
        run: "./my-check.sh"
        working_directory: scripts
        stdout:
          value: "Notification service is ready"
          match:
            type: contains
        trusted_files:
          - scripts/my-check.sh

      # Start a command in the background without waiting for it
      - run: "./my-notification.sh"
        working_directory: scripts
        wait: false
        trusted_files:
          - scripts/my-notification.sh

items.title: Options
items.text: Actions use the command options. The options name, wait and continue_on_error are only available for actions.

items.title: Details
items.text:
Warning

Commands run with the privileges of the user who started PowerRules, so treat policy files like scripts. Use trust to detect modifications.

  • Actions run in the order they are written, in the directory of the policy file by default.
  • If an action fails (unexpected exit code/output, timeout or the command cannot be started), the remaining actions are skipped and the evaluation stops.
  • With continue_on_error: true, a failed action is only logged as a warning and the remaining actions still run. This does not apply to a failed trust check. A modified trusted file always stops the evaluation.
  • With wait: false, the command is started in the background. There is no exit code, no output and no timeout, and the command keeps running if PowerRules ends.
  • Commands can read the name of their rule and action from the environment variables POWERRULES_RULE_NAME and POWERRULES_ACTION_NAME.
  • Actions are not executed with --dry-run.

items.title: Getting Started
items.text: Create, validate, trust and run your first policy.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
pipStandalone binary

Requires Python 3.11 or newer.

pip install powerrules

Download the binary for your platform from the latest release.

Platform Standalone Binary Windows 10/11 powerrules-windows-x86_64.exe Linux powerrules-linux-x86_64powerrules-linux-arm64 macOS powerrules-macos-arm64

Note

pwru is installed by pip. When using a standalone binary, call it by its file name instead.

Check the version:

pwru --version

items.title: Creation
items.text:
Create a file named my-policy.yaml:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LeoTN/PowerRules/main/assets/schema/powerrules_policy.schema.json
# (1)!
rules:
  # Match while no process named "powerrules-demo" is running
  - name: "No demo process is running"
    conditions:
      process:
        name: "powerrules-demo"
        exists: false
    actions:
      - name: "Say hello"
        run: "echo Hello from PowerRules"
  1. Editors with YAML support can use this schema for validation and autocompletion.

items.title: Validation
items.text: pwru policy validate --policy my-policy.yaml

items.title: Trust
items.text:
Review the policy and trust it:

pwru trust add --policy my-policy.yaml

PowerRules refuses to run policies which are not trusted or were modified since, see Trust.

items.title: Execution
items.text:
Use --once to evaluate the policy a single time:

pwru policy run --once --policy my-policy.yaml

INFO     Running policy 'my-policy.yaml' once...
INFO     Policy '/path/to/my-policy.yaml' is trusted
INFO     Running action 'Say hello'
INFO     Action 'Say hello' finished with exit code 0
INFO     Rule 'No demo process is running' matched, executed actions: 'Say hello'

items.title: Policy evaluation
items.text:
Summary

A policy is evaluated continuously or once. Rules are checked from top to bottom, the first matching rule runs its actions, and only when it becomes the active match.

items.title: Example
items.text:
# Evaluate continuously
pwru policy run

# Evaluate every 30 seconds
pwru policy run --interval 30

# Evaluate once and exit
pwru policy run --once

# Only report which rule would match without running any actions
pwru policy run --dry-run

items.title: Evaluation flow
items.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Load policy once] --> B[Check enabled rules from top to bottom]
    B --> C{A rule matches?}
    C -- No --> F[Wait for the interval]
    C -- Yes --> D{Same rule as in the previous evaluation?}
    D -- Yes --> F
    D -- No --> E[Run actions in order]
    E --> F
    F --> B

items.title: Options
items.text:
Option Default Description --policy, -p powerrules.yaml Path to the policy file. --once off Evaluate the policy once and then exit. --interval 10 Seconds between the starts of two evaluations. Has no effect with --once. --stop-on-match off Stop the evaluation after a rule has run its actions. --dry-run off Evaluate the policy without running any action. Commands of command conditions still run. --no-require-trust off Run the policy even if it is not trusted or was modified since it was trusted, see Trust.

Rule options:

Option Default Description name required Name of the rule, used in logs and environment variables. enabled true false skips the rule during evaluation. Trust is still checked.

items.title: Details
items.text:
• A rule runs its actions when it becomes the active match, not on every evaluation while it keeps matching. If another rule or no rule matches in between, the rule runs its actions again the next time it matches.
  • The interval is the time between the starts of two evaluations. If an evaluation takes longer, PowerRules logs a warning and starts the next one immediately.
  • The policy is loaded once at startup, so changes to the file require a restart.
  • Unless --no-require-trust is used, the policy has to be trusted. --dry-run only skips this if the policy has no command condition, because the commands of command conditions run in a dry run as well.
  • If a condition cannot be evaluated, an action fails or a trusted file was modified, the evaluation stops.

items.title: Trust
items.text:
Summary

PowerRules remembers which policies you trust. Every modification of a policy or of its trusted_files makes it untrusted until you trust it again.

items.title: Example
items.text:
# Trust the current content of a policy and its trusted files
pwru trust add --policy my-policy.yaml

# Show all trusted policies and their current status
pwru trust list

# Remove the trust of a policy
pwru trust remove --policy my-policy.yaml

# Remove trusted policies whose policy file no longer exists
pwru trust prune

Scripts and other files which commands depend on are not detected automatically. List them in trusted_files:

actions:
  - run: "./my-action.sh"
    working_directory: scripts
    trusted_files:
      - scripts/my-action.sh # Relative to the policy file (not to working_directory)

items.title: Options
items.text: Command Options Description trust add --policy Trust the current content of the policy and its trusted files. An invalid policy or an unreadable file cannot be trusted. trust remove --policy Remove the trust of the policy. trust list --trusted, --modified, --missing List all trusted policies and their current status. Several filters can be combined, a policy is shown if it matches at least one. trust prune --dry-run, --yes, -y Remove trusted policies whose policy file no longer exists. --dry-run only shows what would be removed, --yes skips the confirmation.

items.title: Details
items.text:
Warning

Trust only covers the policy and its trusted_files. Programs started by commands are not checked and the trust store is only protected by the permissions of your user account.

  • A policy is identified by its path and trusted by its content (SHA-256 hash).
  • pwru policy run refuses to run untrusted policies by default. --no-require-trust overrides this.
  • The policy and its trusted files are checked when the policy is loaded. Right before an action or a command condition runs, its trusted_files are checked again.
  • A policy only counts as trusted if the policy and all of its trusted files are trusted.
  • The trust store is saved in ~/.powerrules/trust.json.

items.title: Trust status of the policy and its files
items.text: Status Description trusted The content is unchanged since it was trusted. unknown The policy or file was never trusted. modified The content changed since it was trusted. missing The file cannot be read.

items.title: Conditions
items.text:
Summary

Conditions decide whether a rule matches. They check processes, windows, the time or the result of a command and can be combined with and, or and not.

items.title: Example
items.text:
rules:
  # Match on weekends while no backup process is running
  - name: "Weekend without backup"
    conditions:
      and:
        - datetime:
            weekday:
              - "Saturday"
              - "Sunday"
        - process:
            name: "backup" #(1)!
            exists: false
    actions:
      - run: "echo Weekend without backup"
  1. Consider using contains or regex matching for different platforms.

Every rule has exactly one conditions entry. To check several things, combine them with a logical condition.

items.title: Condition types
items.text:
Condition Matches when Notes process a process with the given name exists or does not exist window a window with the given title exists or does not exist Availability depends on the platform datetime the current date, time, weekday or month fits Uses the local time of the computer command the exit code and the output of a command fit Also runs with --dry-run and, or, not the combination of other conditions fits

process, window and command compare text with match types: exact, regular expression or contains.

items.title: Details
items.text:
• Conditions are evaluated on every evaluation of the policy.
  • and and or stop at the first decisive result, so the remaining conditions might not run.
  • If a condition cannot be evaluated (e.g. a command exceeds its timeout or window conditions are not available on the platform), the evaluation stops.

items.title: Related
items.text:
• Policy Evaluation

    Continuous evaluation and --dry-run.

  • Actions

    Run commands when a rule matches.

  • Trust

    Detect modifications of policies and scripts.

items.title: Command
items.text:
Summary

Matches if a command finishes with a successful exit code and the configured output. Command conditions also run with --dry-run.

items.title: Example
items.text:
WindowsLinux & macOS 
rules:
  # Match if the script exits with 0 or 2 and prints "successful" (case-sensitive)
  - name: "Check is successful"
    conditions:
      command:
        run: '.\my-check.ps1'
        working_directory: scripts # Relative to the policy file
        success_exit_codes: [0, 2]
        stdout:
          value: "successful"
          match:
            type: contains
        trusted_files:
          - scripts/my-check.ps1 # Relative to the policy file (not to working_directory)
    actions:
      - run: "echo Check is successful"

rules:
  # Match if the script exits with 0 or 2 and prints "successful" (case-insensitive)
  - name: "Check is successful"
    conditions:
      command:
        run: "./my-check.sh"
        working_directory: scripts # Relative to the policy file
        success_exit_codes: [0, 2]
        stdout:
          value: "successful"
          match:
            type: contains
            case_sensitive: false
        trusted_files:
          - scripts/my-check.sh # Relative to the policy file (not to working_directory)
    actions:
      - run: "echo Check is successful"

items.title: Options
items.text: Command conditions use the command options.

items.title: Details
items.text:
Warning

Command conditions run on every evaluation, even with --dry-run. Use trust to detect modifications.

  • The condition matches if the exit code and all configured outputs match. A different exit code or output is no error, the condition simply does not match.
  • If the command cannot be started or exceeds its timeout, the condition cannot be evaluated and the evaluation stops.
  • Unlike actions, conditions do not receive the POWERRULES_* environment variables.
  • Commands and their output are only logged on DEBUG level.
  • and and or stop at the first decisive result. Put cheap conditions first, so the command only runs when needed.

See Actions vs. command conditions for the differences to the commands of actions.

items.title: Related
items.text:
• Policy Evaluation

    Continuous evaluation and --dry-run.

  • Actions

  • Trust

    Detect modifications of policies and scripts.

items.title: Datetime
items.text:
Summary

Matches a time of day, an absolute date range, weekdays or months. All values use the local time of the computer.

items.title: Example
items.text:
rules:
  # Match on Saturday and Sunday nights in August from 22:00 until 6:00 the next morning
  - name: "Weekend night in August"
    conditions:
      datetime:
        between:
          start: "22"
          end: "6"
        weekday:
          - "Saturday"
          - "Sunday"
        month:
          - "August"
    actions:
      - run: "echo Weekend night in August"

More examples:

# Match every day from 23:00 until 1:30 the next morning
- datetime:
    between:
      start: "23"
      end: "1:30"

# Match on Mondays and Fridays
- datetime:
    weekday: ["Monday", "Friday"]

# Match on the whole days 2026-08-21 and 2026-08-22
- datetime:
    between:
      start: "2026-08-21"
      end: "2026-08-23"

# Match from 2026-08-21 18:00 until 2026-08-23 6:00
- datetime:
    between:
      start: "2026-08-21 18:00"
      end: "2026-08-23 6:00"

items.title: Options
items.text:
At least one of between, weekday and month is required. If several are configured, all of them have to match.

Option Default Description between none Range in which the condition matches. start and end must be of the same kind (see below). weekday none List of English weekday names (case-insensitive), e.g. Monday. month none List of English month names (case-insensitive), e.g. January.

Kinds of between:

Kind Format Example Description Time of day H, HH, H:MM, HH:MM, H:MM:SS or HH:MM:SS "23", "1:30" Repeats every day and may cross midnight. Date YYYY-MM-DD "2026-08-21" Covers whole days, from 0:00 of the start date until 0:00 of the end date. Date with time YYYY-MM-DD followed by a space or T and a time "2026-08-21 18:00" Absolute range without timezone.

items.title: Details
items.text:
• The start of a range is inclusive, the end is exclusive.
  • If a time range crosses midnight, weekday and month refer to the day on which the range starts. With 23 to 1:30 and Monday, the condition matches from Monday 23:00 until Tuesday 1:30.
  • For absolute ranges, weekday and month refer to the current day. With 2026-08-21 18:00 to 2026-08-23 6:00 and Friday, the condition only matches on Friday from 18:00 until midnight, because the weekday changes to Saturday at 0:00.
  • Timezones are not supported.

items.title: Related
items.text:
• Policy Evaluation

    Continuous evaluation and --dry-run.

  • Actions

    Run commands when a rule matches.

  • Trust

    Detect modifications of policies and scripts.

items.title: Logical
items.text:
Summary

Combines other conditions with and, or and not. They can be nested as deeply as needed.

items.title: Example
items.text:
rules:
  # Match in December or January, but not on weekends, while VLC is running
  - name: "Winter weekday with VLC"
    conditions:
      and:
        - or: #(1)!
            - datetime:
                month:
                  - "December"
            - datetime:
                month:
                  - "January"
        - not:
            datetime:
              weekday:
                - "Saturday"
                - "Sunday"
        - process:
            name: "vlc" #(2)!
            exists: true
    actions:
      - run: "echo Winter weekday with VLC"

  1. Using or like this is a more elaborate way of writing:

    month: ["December", "January"]

    but you get the idea.

  2. Consider using contains or regex matching for different platforms.

items.title: Options
items.text: Option Takes Matches when and list of at least two conditions all conditions match. or list of at least two conditions at least one condition matches. not exactly one condition the condition does not match.

items.title: Details
items.text:
• A condition defines exactly one of and, or, not or a single condition type.
  • and and or evaluate their conditions in order and stop at the first decisive result. In other words, if an and condition finds a non-matching condition, it stops and returns false. If an or condition finds a matching condition, it stops and returns true.
  • not only negates the result. If the inner condition cannot be evaluated, the evaluation still stops.

items.title: Related
items.text:
• Policy Evaluation

    Continuous evaluation and --dry-run.

  • Actions

    Run commands when a rule matches.

  • Trust

    Detect modifications of policies and scripts.

items.title: Process
items.text:
Summary

Matches while a process with the given name exists or does not exist. The name is compared with a match type.

items.title: Example
items.text:
WindowsLinux & macOS 
rules:
  # Match while Firefox is running
  - name: "Firefox is running"
    conditions:
      process:
        name: "firefox.exe"
        exists: true
    actions:
      - run: "echo Firefox is running"

rules:
  # Match while Firefox is running
  - name: "Firefox is running"
    conditions:
      process:
        name: "firefox"
        exists: true
    actions:
      - run: "echo Firefox is running"

items.title: Options
items.text: Option Default Description name required Name of the process to check. exists required Whether the process is expected to exist (true) or not (false). match exact, case-sensitive How the name is matched, see Match Types.

items.title: Details
items.text: • Process names usually differ between platforms (e.g. firefox.exe on Windows, firefox on Linux and macOS). Use a contains or regex match to write one policy for several platforms.

items.title: Related
items.text:
• Policy Evaluation

    Continuous evaluation and --dry-run.

  • Actions

    Run commands when a rule matches.

  • Trust

    Detect modifications of policies and scripts.

items.title: Window
items.text:
Summary

Matches while a window with the given title exists or does not exist. Availability depends on the platform.

items.title: Example
items.text:
rules:
  # Match while a window title contains "Mozilla Firefox" (case-sensitive)
  - name: "Firefox window is open"
    conditions:
      window:
        title: "Mozilla Firefox"
        exists: true
        match:
          type: contains
    actions:
      - run: "echo Firefox window is open"

items.title: Options
items.text: Option Default Description title required Title of the window to check. exists required Whether the window is expected to exist (true) or not (false). match exact, case-sensitive How the title is matched, see Match Types.

items.title: Details
items.text:
Only windows with a non-empty title are checked. Minimized windows are included.

Platform Requirement Windows PowerRules has to run in the session of the logged-in user, not as a service. Windows on other virtual desktops and suspended UWP apps are skipped. Linux An X11 session with a window manager which provides a window list. Wayland is not supported. macOS The screen recording permission is required.

If a requirement is not met, window conditions cannot be evaluated and the evaluation stops.

items.title: Related
items.text:
• Policy Evaluation

    Continuous evaluation and --dry-run.

  • Actions

    Run commands when a rule matches.

  • Trust

    Detect modifications of policies and scripts.

items.title: Command options
items.text:
Summary

Options which actions and command conditions have in common. They define which command runs, how it runs and what counts as success.

items.title: Options
items.text:
Options without a label apply to actions and command conditions. Actions only marks options which command conditions do not have.

Option Default Description run required Command to run. A command with several lines stops at the first failing line. name Actions only Action N of M Name of the action, used in log messages. shell powershell on Windows, sh on Linux and macOS One of sh, bash, cmd, powershell or pwsh. The shell has to be installed. working_directory directory of the policy file Relative paths are resolved against the directory of the policy file. env none Additional environment variables. Numbers and booleans are converted to strings. Names starting with POWERRULES_ are reserved. timeout 60 Maximum run time in seconds. Afterwards, the command and its child processes are terminated. null or .inf disables the limit. success_exit_codes [0] Exit codes which count as success. stdout, stderr none Expected output of the command. A different output counts as unsuccessful (see below). wait Actions only true false starts the command in the background. Cannot be combined with timeout, success_exit_codes, stdout or stderr. continue_on_error Actions only false Whether the remaining actions still run if this action fails. trusted_files none Files (e.g. scripts) the command depends on. They are verified before every run. Relative paths are resolved against the directory of the policy file.

Options of stdout and stderr:

Option Default Description value required Text or regular expression the output is compared with. match exact, case-sensitive How the output is matched, see Match Types.

items.title: Details
items.text:
• The output is compared after leading and trailing whitespace was removed.
  • The shell cmd only supports a single line. Chain commands with && instead.
  • trusted_files are relative to the policy file, not to working_directory. See Trust.

items.title: Actions vs. command conditions
items.text: Situation Action Command condition Unexpected exit code or output The action fails and the remaining actions are skipped unless continue_on_error is set. The condition does not match. Command cannot be started or times out The action fails. The evaluation stops. POWERRULES_RULE_NAME, POWERRULES_ACTION_NAME Set. Not set. --dry-run Not executed. Executed.

items.title: Exit codes
items.text:
Summary

pwru reports the result of a command via its exit code.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Validating a policy file which does not exist ends with exit code 2:

Linux and macOS (sh)Windows (PowerShell) 
pwru policy validate --policy missing.yaml
echo $?

pwru policy validate --policy missing.yaml
echo $LASTEXITCODE

ERROR    Policy file not found: /path/to/missing.yaml
2

items.title: Exit codes
items.text:
Contributions welcome

This part of PowerRules needs improvement. Feel free to open an issue or submit a pull request on GitHub.

Exit code Meaning Examples 0 Success. The policy is valid, was evaluated or no rule matched. 1 Runtime error. A condition cannot be evaluated, an action fails, the trust store cannot be read or written, an unexpected error occurred or a confirmation was declined (trust prune). 2 Policy error or invalid usage. The policy file was not found, contains invalid YAML or fails validation. Invalid command line options also use this code. 3 Trust error. The policy or one of its trusted_files is not trusted, was modified or cannot be read, see Trust.

items.title: Logging
items.text:
Summary

Messages are shown on the console and written to a rotating log file. Commands of actions and command conditions and their output are only logged on DEBUG level.

items.title: Example
items.text: pwru policy run --log-level DEBUG --log-file my-log.log

items.title: Options
items.text:
All policy and trust commands accept these options:

Option Default Description --log-level INFO Minimum log level shown on the console and written to the log file. One of DEBUG, INFO, WARNING or ERROR. --log-file powerrules.log Path to the rotating log file. --log-level-file value of --log-level Minimum log level written to the log file.

items.title: Details
items.text:
• Messages below WARNING are written to stdout, WARNING and ERROR to stderr.
  • The log file is rotated at 10 MB and five backups are kept.
  • Use --log-level DEBUG to find out why a condition did or did not match.

items.title: Match types
items.text:
Summary

Process names, window titles and command output can be matched exactly, with a regular expression or by a part of the text. Regular expressions use full-string matching.

items.title: Example
items.text:
# Match if the process name contains "fire"
- process:
    name: "fire"
    exists: true
    match:
      type: contains
      case_sensitive: true # This is the default

# Match if the window title starts with "firefox" (case-insensitive)
- window:
    title: "Firefox.*"
    exists: true
    match:
      type: regex
      case_sensitive: false

items.title: Options
items.text:
Options of match:

Option Default Description type exact Matching mode: exact, regex (full-string match) or contains (part of the text). case_sensitive true Whether uppercase and lowercase letters are treated differently.

items.title: Details
items.text:
• Match types are available for the process and window conditions and for the stdout and stderr of commands.
  • A regular expression has to match the whole value. fire does not match firefox, but fire.* does.
  • A . in a regular expression also matches line breaks, so patterns work on multi-line output.
  • The output of a command is compared after leading and trailing whitespace was removed.
